If you ever come to Sydney, I strongly recommend a walk around the CBD against the harbour (Darling Harbour down to the Rocks, around to Circular Quay, past the Botanical Gardens, around Mrs Macquarie's Chair, then back through the Domain and Hyde Park). It takes about 2-3 hours to walk it (longer if you stop along the way - and there is plenty to stop and see!) If you wanted a shorter version, I'd recommend going through Hyde Park, past St Mary's Cathedral (even if you're not religious, just check out the beautiful sandstone and architecture), through the Botanical Gardens and around Mrs Macquarie's Chair.

Obviously there are the standard tourist sites, but there are also some better ways to see them. For example, rather than just seeing the Sydney Harbour Bridge, do the 'bridge climb'; be warned though, if you're scared of heights, don't do this (there's a spot where you are literally walking over two shitty wooden planks over a 200' drop because they haven't repaired the scaffolding yet). When you go to see the Opera House, it's worth grabbing a pint down at the Opera Bar (some of the best views for any bar in Sydney, as you can sit right against the water's edge). If you want a view over the city there is the Centrepoint Tower - if you want to spend longer looking at the view, it has a revolving restaurant (the food's pretty average, but the view is fantastic). I'd also recommend going out to our old Quarantine Station for a ghost tour - great for the kids, but also a decent history lesson and a fantastic atmosphere.

Bear in mind that the only difference between a male and female is 1 chromosome in 46. Because of diploidy, the broad (and simplified) effect of this is that males can express certain proteins females can't, and that females have redundancy (robustness) in their allosomes, along with being able to express higher concentrations of the proteins there encoded (what difference the concentrations make is complex and requires biochemical consideration). Also bear in mind that the linkage from genes to phenotypic properties is often complicated/confounded (e.g. multigenic traits, epigenetic factors, etc.).

In short, I'm not aware of any particular genes that are known to cause the affect you are interested in. If someone else knows of some, though, I would be very interested to read the literature on it.

It certainly does make a difference - I suppose my point was more to quantify how much of one. There are about 450 genes on the Y chromosome, out of ~25,000 genes total in our genome; ignoring genes found on both X and Y chromosomes along with other complexities (duplicates, alternate splicing, etc.) that's about a 2% difference. Of course, my analysis there is deliberately naïve - a single mutation can have a profound effect on development, not to mention that we differ from some other species by less than 2% of our coding regions.

Without knowing the function of all of those genes, we could still approach this question from the perspective of evolution / mate selection. If there was a preference for a given biological gender to perform a given role, then it would be selected for (i.e. all things being equal, those who were better at it would more frequently be taken as mates, consequently would have more offspring). Generally/simplistically speaking (at least to the best of my knowledge), the chromosome on which a mutation develops that contributes to a particular phenotypic trait is largely random. If a given trait is advantageous to one biological gender and disadvantageous to the other, and given humans only produce a small number of offspring, then its presence on an autosome would mute any selection bias for it. Effectively it would likely have to be present on an allosome (sex chromosome) in order to be consistently selected for across generations. On the other hand, if the trait was not disadvantageous to the other biological gender, it wouldn't matter which chromosome it was present on. In short, if you wanted to make the case that a given gene was present on an allosome and predisposed females to being better at housework, you would need to conclude that the same gene is somehow disadvantageous to males.

Another thing to consider, though, is that evolutionary timescales are very large (thousands to millions of years, generally speaking). Civilization as we know it has really only been around for about 10,000 years, which arguably wouldn't have been enough time for such a trait to develop. That said, I believe there is evidence for distinct gender roles in hunter-gatherer societies (anthropology isn't one of my fields, so I have no idea how strong this evidence is), so possibly any genetic selection could have leveraged/piggy-backed on this.

It might be worth cross posting your question to /v/AskScience but I would suggest trying to be as neutral/broad as possible in your phrasing so that it isn't dismissed without consideration.
